title: Where Is the Work?
theme: The identity of an artwork across repetition, reconstruction, changes of medium, and digital creation.
ordering: Historical arc using the ancient type, conception, cast or reconstruction dates relevant to each comparison; captions distinguish these layers.
interpretation: Curatorial comparisons among distinct historical uses of repetition, without a proposed single lineage or claim that a digital representation has the same status as a physical artwork.

works.title: Cylinder Seal
works.caption: 3300–2900 BCE. A carved cylinder is an image waiting to happen. Rolled over a soft surface, it transfers its design into an impression; the small object can generate a much longer field of images. Begin with a distinction that runs through the exhibition: the thing that holds a form and the places where that form appears.

works.title: Athena Lemnia
works.caption: Ancient type, c. 440 BCE; later reconstruction and plaster cast. The apparent unity of this figure is an argument. SMK identifies it as Furtwängler’s reconstruction combining a torso in Dresden with the Palagi head in Bologna. What looks like one surviving statue brings separate pieces together through an interpretation. The digital view adds another stage to that history.

works.title: Buddha, Gandhara
works.caption: 3rd century CE. The flowing robe and modeled features connect this Gandharan Buddha with Greek and Roman visual traditions, as Mia’s museum record explains. A borrowed sculptural vocabulary serves a different religious image. Here originality becomes a question of transformation: what happens when familiar forms acquire another purpose?

works.title: Madonna and Child
works.caption: Second quarter of the 14th century; the museum queries its status as a replica. This figure repeats the type and form of the venerated Madonna at Altötting. Its relationship to another image is part of its significance. The later crown, right hand and base also complicate the boundary between a work’s first state and the object that survives.

works.title: Faun with Cymbals
works.caption: Model 1783–1784; porcelain made 1784–1814. This small faun repeats an ancient composition preserved in Florence. Jüchtzer’s model and the Meissen manufactory’s production are separate acts, with separate dates. The familiar opposition between an original and a copy gives way to a longer chain: inherited composition, new model, manufactured object, digital scan.

works.title: The Age of Bronze
works.caption: Conceived 1877; this bronze cast before 1941. Rodin’s figure looked so lifelike that critics accused him of casting directly from a living body. He had to demonstrate that he had modeled it. The dispute exposes a revealing distinction: a bronze cast could count as sculpture, while a suspected life cast threatened its artistic standing. The method changed the judgment.

works.title: Plaster Cast of False Pediment of Room for Dancers of Ta Prohm
works.caption: 1888–1889 plaster cast after a medieval Khmer relief. A plaster reproduction carries part of Cambodian temple architecture into a museum in Paris. Plaster carries the carved form into a new material and setting; this scan carries it again. What remains accessible is the relief’s surface. Its architectural surroundings and the experience of encountering it at Ta Prohm cannot travel in the same way.

works.title: Incomplete Open Cube 6/8
works.caption: 1974. LeWitt makes a system visible by removing edges from a cube. This particular arrangement belongs to a larger investigation of possible incomplete structures. The work asks us to attend to decisions and relationships as well as material. Atrium shows a later digital reconstruction: the arrangement can be represented again, while the physical sculpture remains a distinct object.

works.title: Two Reclining Figures on a Calder Base
works.caption: 2006–2018. Rogiers openly names his debt to Calder in the title and reworks the long tradition of reclining figures. Quotation becomes a means of making something new. This digital version adds a further complication: it conveys the sculpture’s shapes but omits its vivid blue finish. How much can change before we feel we are encountering a different work?

works.title: Asad Al-Lat (Lion of Al-Lat)
works.date: early 1st century CE original; 2015 digital reconstruction
works.caption: 2015 digital reconstruction of an early 1st-century sculpture. Georges Dahdouh’s model for New Palmyra responds to the violent damage of the Lion of Al-Lat. A reconstruction makes the form available to study and share, while also recording a later act of interpretation. The file preserves access to an image; the ancient stone, its history and its losses remain another matter.

works.title: Africhibi: Aimasai
works.caption: Published 2022. Nairobi Design Week’s Aimasai draws on Kenyan soapstone sculpture and African jewelry, but begins here as a digitally modeled character. The exhibition ends with a reversal: a file can be a creative work in its own medium, as well as a representation of something elsewhere. Cultural references continue to travel even when there is no scanned physical original.
